query_text: What medicine should I take when I get a cold?

message.content:
Based on the search results, here's what you should know about treating a cold:

## Important Facts About Colds

**There is no cure for the common cold.** No medication can cure a cold or shorten its duration (typically 7-10 days). Medications only provide symptom relief while the cold runs its course.

## Over-the-Counter Medications for Symptom Relief

### For Nasal Congestion (Stuffy Nose)
- **Decongestants** like **pseudoephedrine** (Sudafed) can help reduce swelling in nasal blood vessels and make breathing easier
- **Nasal sprays** with oxymetazoline (Afrin) or phenylephrine can provide quick relief
- **Important:** Don't use nasal decongestant sprays for more than 3-4 days, as they can cause "rebound congestion" that makes symptoms worse

**Note:** In November 2024, the FDA proposed removing **oral phenylephrine** as an active ingredient because it was found to be ineffective as a nasal decongestant (though safe). Nasal sprays containing phenylephrine are still considered effective.

### For Pain and Fever
- **Acetaminophen** (Tylenol)
- **Ibuprofen** (Advil, Motrin)
- These can help with headaches, sore throat, and fever

### For Cough
- **Dextromethorphan** is a common cough suppressant in many cold medicines
- **Honey** (for adults and children over age 1) may help coughs when added to warm tea or lemon water

### What Doesn't Work Well
- **Antihistamines** are generally **not very effective** for cold symptoms, though they may provide short-term relief for some people
- **Antibiotics** do NOT work for colds (colds are caused by viruses, not bacteria)

## Non-Drug Remedies That Help

- **Stay hydrated** – water, juice, clear broth, or warm lemon water with honey
- **Rest** – your body needs energy to fight the infection
- **Warm liquids** – chicken soup, tea, or warm apple juice may ease stuffiness
- **Saline nasal drops/sprays** – safe and effective for relieving congestion
- **Saltwater gargle** – for sore throat relief (¼ to ½ teaspoon salt in 8 oz warm water)
- **Humidifier or cool-mist vaporizer** – adds moisture to air to ease stuffiness

## Important Warnings

- **Children under 4** should NOT take OTC cold medicines containing antihistamines or decongestants due to risk of serious side effects
- **Never give aspirin to children or teenagers** – linked to Reye's syndrome
- **Don't give honey to children under 1 year old**
- If you have **high blood pressure or heart disease**, check with your doctor before taking decongestants
- Read labels carefully to avoid accidentally taking too much of the same ingredient (especially acetaminophen) across multiple products

## When to See a Doctor

- Symptoms last more than 10 days or worsen
- High fever (above 101.3°F or 38.5°C)
- Severe headache, sinus pain, or earache
- Difficulty breathing or chest pain

**Always consult with a healthcare provider if you're unsure which medications are safe for you, especially if you have other health conditions or take other medications.**

Sources:
1. https://apps.who.int/iris/bitstream/10665/66856/1/WHO_FCH_CAH_01.02.pdf
2. https://www.webmd.com/cold-and-flu/decongestants-antihistamines-cold
3. https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/drugs/24923-nasal-decongestant
4. https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/common-cold/in-depth/cold-remedies/art-20046403
